extracted.intended_audience: USPTO TC1600 patent examiners (examining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on drafting and supporting rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness), including the required factual findings, acceptable rationales for combining or modifying prior art, and how those rationales must be tied to the facts of the application and cited references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis for obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting AIA 35 U.S.C. 103: 'Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.' Use this statutory standard as the foundation for any 103 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. Deere factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103, consider the Graham factors: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the prior art and the claimed invention; (3) level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) objective evidence relevant to obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four factual inquiries (see MPEP 2141 (II)) must be considered and supported with findings of fact when making an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address findings of fact and provide a rationale for combining/modifying references
rubrics_metrics.description: Any 103 rejection must address findings of fact and then provide a rationale for combining or modifying the references relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each rejection must contain an explicit rationale clearly explaining why it would have been obvious to combine or modify the teachings of the references. Each included claim must be explicitly addressed in the rejection, although it is not necessary to rewrite the entire rejection for each claim. (See MPEP 2143.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why the person of ordinary skill would have made the modification
rubrics_metrics.description: For each rationale used, examiners must explain why the person of ordinary skill in the art would have found the proposed modification obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions unaccompanied by a reasoned statement are insufficient to establish a prima facie case. This explanation is required for every obviousness rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior-art elements to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: A permissible rationale is combining prior art elements according to known methods where the combination yields predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that the elements perform their known functions and that a skilled artisan would have expected the combined outcome (example illustrated by combining Patent A's method with Patent B's high-pressure washing). See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness may be supported by substituting a known element with another known element when a skilled artisan would have expected predictable results from the substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the substituted element is known to be suitable and why the substitution would be expected to work (e.g., substituting ofloxacin for ciprofloxacin because both are gyrase inhibitors known suitable for otic use). See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of known technique to improve similar devices/methods/products
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to improve similar devices, methods, or products in the same way can be a valid rationale for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie the known technique and the similar device together and explain the expectation of improved results based on the prior art teachings. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (or method/product) that is ready for improvement to yield predictable results is an acceptable rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the device was 'ready for improvement' and that the technique would have been predictably applicable. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions ('obvious to try')
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting from a finite set of predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success can support an obviousness finding ('obvious to try').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the solutions were finite and predictable and why a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in the same or a different field
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior work in one field may prompt predictable variations for use in the same or different field based on design incentives or market forces if those variations are predictable to a skilled artisan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how design incentives or market forces and predictability would have motivated the skilled artisan to make the variation. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led a skilled artisan to modify or combine references to arrive at the claimed invention is an appropriate rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the teaching/suggestion/motivation in the references and explain how it would have led to the claimed modification or combination. See MPEP 2143 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping, approaching, and similar ranges/amounts/proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: When claimed ranges overlap or lie within prior-art ranges a prima facie case of obviousness exists; when ranges are merely close a prima facie case may also exist, but examiners must explain why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must explain why the claimed ranges in each included claim overlap or are close to the prior art's ranges. Dependent claim ranges must also be particularly explained as necessary. See MPEP 2144.05 (I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimization within prior-art conditions or routine experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine optimization (e.g., adjusting concentrations, temperatures) generally will not support patentability unless an articulated rationale shows why routine optimization would have led to the claimed invention with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide findings of relevant facts and underpinning reasoning in sufficient detail. The presence of a result-effective variable can be a motivation to optimize, but examiners must explain why routine optimization would have been performed and successful. See MPEP 2144.05 (II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-recognized equivalence for same purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If the art recognizes two compositions or processes as useful individually for the same purpose, combining them may be prima facie obvious, but the examiner must explain the art's recognition of each utility as of the relevant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the art recognized the equivalence before the effective filing date; mere functional or mechanical equivalence is insufficient if the art did not recognize that equivalence. See MPEP 2144.06.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales relying on common knowledge and official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may rely on common knowledge in the art without providing a reference, but must provide a clear and unmistakable line of technical reasoning; statements unsupported by documentary evidence qualify as official notice and are appropriate only for facts capable of instant and unquestionable demonstration as well-known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible, cite a reference to support technical or scientific statements. It is never appropriate to rely on common knowledge as the principal evidence for a rejection; 'common sense' or 'intuitive' conclusions absent articulated rationale are insufficient. See MPEP 2144.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: When relying on legal precedent, show application to the facts and not rely solely on case law
rubrics_metrics.description: Case law can supply a line of reasoning to support an obviousness finding, but the examiner must show how that line of reasoning applies to the facts of the application at hand and case law should not be the sole basis for obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide fact-specific explanation tying the precedent to the claimed limitations. Common TC1600 examples include automating a manual activity, changes in size/shape/sequence of adding ingredients, purifying an old product. See MPEP 2144.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie the selected rationale to the facts of the case and each claimed limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection must explain why the invention as a whole and the limitations of each included claim would have been obvious over the cited prior art, and must explain how the selected rationale applies to the facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, fact-specific rejections permit applicants, examiners, and reviewers to understand the basis for rejection. Examiners should explain that at least one particular rationale applies and map that rationale to the claim limitations. (Summary and multiple example slides.)
